# The appointments Nishinakahime made — and who is keeping them

One myth is a story. A cycle of myths is a specification. Read Nishinakahime's cycle in order and the industries fall out of it one by one.

## At a Glance

- **Temple:** Nishinakahime
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Domain of influence:** Rice, Agriculture
- **Pattern seats:** 3
- **Sectors touched:** Energy & Natural World · Home & Lifestyle · Health & Wellbeing
- **Strongest seat:** Agriculture, Food & Harvest
- **Series:** The Resonance Files, No. 343 of 546

## The Cycle, Read Forward

### Agriculture, Food & Harvest — through *The Dying Goddess Bears the Clay Kami*

Izanami gave birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi, and the fire burned her so badly that she sickened and lay dying.  From her body in its extremity came the last kami of the living generation: from her vomit, the metal-mountain deities Kanayamahiko and Kanayamahime; from her urine, the water goddess Mizuha-no-me; and from her bowels, the brother and sister of clay — Hani-yasu-biko and Hani-yasu-hime (Kojiki, birth of Kagutsuchi; the Nihon Shoki gives her the parallel names Haniyama-hime, 'Clay-Mountain Princess,' and Haniyasu-no-kami).

The atlas states the seat in one line: *The day-sun wave princess of rice and agriculture; the crop is her court.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. Industries do not invent their archetypes; they inherit them and call them best practice.

### Food & Hospitality — through *A Name That Means 'Clay That Yields'*

Hani-yasu is a name that explains itself, the way kami names so often do.  Hani (埴) is potter's clay, the earth dug from the subsoil that holds water and takes any shape; yasu (安/易) is 'easy, gentle, workable.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *The rice princess; the harvest is the first course.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. The trade thinks it is optimizing a process. It is re-enacting a charter.

### Yoga, Meditation & Holistic Wellness — through *Three Gifts of Civilization from One Body*

Read together, the kami born from Izanami's failing body form a complete inventory of material culture.  Kanayama-hime, from the vomit, is metal — ore, smelting, the smith's art.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *The rice princess as nourishment and sustenance; the calm of the full granary.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. The trade thinks it is optimizing a process. It is re-enacting a charter.

## The Theme That Runs the Cycle

Nishinakahime's mythology is two sentences long in the Kojiki — and they are among the most striking in the whole canon. Everything else the tradition knows about her is in her name: hani, potter's clay, and yasu, the yielding. The potters of Japan's ancient kiln towns supplied the rest of her story — a thousand years of practice laid at her feet.

## The Method, Stated Plainly

The atlas is not a horoscope. Seats are earned from the sources — argued, weighted, published — and every one of them can be challenged at the [methodology page](/patterns/methodology/). A match that cannot survive an argument does not survive review. That is the whole trick: the patterns are claims, and claims can be tested.

## For the Ones Who Work There

If you work in agriculture, food & harvest, food & hospitality, or any trade this temple holds a seat in, this is the honest version of what a placement means: your industry beside the story it has been re-telling all along — on the temple floor itself, before an audience that came specifically to read it. The [patron tier](/nishinakahime/patron/) and the [advertising terms](/terms/advertising/) describe the mechanics; the resonance above describes the fit.
